[h1]An enjoyable lack of planning[/h1]

This game is kind of a mixed bag. Overall, I've enjoyed the experience. There are a lot of systems that feel lazily thrown in that can ruin the experience if you're counting on using them. The game's core loop of farming works very well. You start simple with a small farm, interact with the town's people, learn new things you can make to simplify farming, collect materials in the mines and by foraging. You them use these materials to build things that make farming easier.

[h2]The mines[/h2]

Honestly, I'm not a fan of the actual farming. I was really intrigued by the mines at first. I delved into them and was disappointed by what I felt was a lack of depth (gameplay depth, not mine levels depth). The combat isn't challenging, the mines don't actually hold any especially cool secrets. The reward for getting to the bottom is underwhelming, etc. There are several other mine-like places in the games that I enjoy more.

The game relies a lot on the luck system and RNG to give you content in the mines. On one side, this provides variety when delving into these dungeons. On the other hand, my success in these dungeons felt more like it was up to chance than it was something I could control to a satisfying degree.

[h2]Introducing multiplayer to my experience[/h2]

Because I don't much enjoy the farming aspect, multiplayer means my wife and I can enjoy different aspects of the game together. At least, that's what it means on the surface. Multiplayer has some quirks in regards to the mines. In single player, eating food, browsing your inventory, and several other actions all pause the game. The balance of difficulty seems to rely pretty heavily on the fact that doing these things pauses the game. In multiplayer however, the game only pauses if all players are performing one of these pausing actions simultaneously. In the mines, this means that enemies keep moving while you are eating or drinking to restore health or energy. This would be fine, except for how heavily the game relies on the pausing for it to be balanced. Enemies don't just keep moving, this means they all pile on top of you while you eat and do damage the instant you are no longer in the animation.

On top of the increased difficulty of combat, the mines are also balanced around you being able to spend more time there. There are challenges you can choose to engage in that are like "descend x levels in x days in these mines". In single player, time slows down to give you the time necessary to make that descent. In multi-player, the same change applies here as it did to creatures in the game. The game only slows time if [i]all[/i] players are in the mines together. This adds difficulty the game isn't really balanced around.

[h2]Learning the game's secrets[/h2]

The game has a lot of complex systems and a lot of content that isn't immediately obvious how to use, or even how to learn to use. If you just enjoy exploring the mechanics and how they work through trial and error, I don't expect you will have the same trouble with this that I do. I am confident, however, that it will take you a long time to learn of all the locations, secrets, tools, etc. that are available to you. I've had to rely pretty heavily on the stardew valley wiki to learn things about this game. Some systems seem to have limited impact on the game until you reach some unknown milestone. Without a wiki to tell me "Yes, there is a reason you should keep doing that thing" I would have chosen not to care about some systems and missed out on a lot of content.

[h2]In summary[/h2]

Overall, the game still has fun aspects. Depending on how you play, the issues I've encountered might not bother you often enough for you to notice. I do enjoy playing this game, and all my criticism comes from a place of loving it. The game has fun unique characters and systems that give it a lot of charm. Interacting with the characters in this game and learning their stories is a joy. Just be aware that if you're counting on enjoying some of these aspects of the game I've listed, especially in a multiplayer experience, make sure there are other parts of the game you enjoy enough for it to still be fun. Or maybe play with someone who enjoys the same things you do, so you can go to places like the mines together regularly.

Le jeu possède plusieurs activités que vous pouvez réaliser pour passer le temps comme l'agriculture, la pêche ou l'extraction minière. Cependant, je trouve très difficile de faire une grosse session de jeu car c'est pas si intéressant à long terme.

Le jeu peut être jugé intéressant pour son aspect social. Il y'a de mémoire 28 PNJ dans la petite commune où vous vivez et vous pouvez parler avec chacun d'eux. Ils possèdent chacun leurs propres personnalités et vous pouvez leurs offrir des cadeaux pour monter dans leur estime et devenir amis avec eux. Je trouve personnellement cet aspect du jeu inintéressant, on passe notre temps à essayer d'offrir des cadeaux à chaque personnage en fonction de leurs préferences. Contrairement à ce que l'on pourrait penser, on n'a pas de réel dialogue avec les personnages, on ne peut pas choisir quoi leur dire ou de quoi parle. Limitant fortement les interactions disponibles.

En conclusion, je pense clairement que ce jeu n'est pas fait pour moi. J'ai trouvé la boucle de gameplay inintéressante et ennuyante (C'est à dire une des activités + parler et offrir aux PNJ). Il y a des tentatives de redynamiser le gameplay, notamment avec les évènements mais ils sauvent à peine les meubles. Je ne prends aucun plaisir à jouer au jeu mais si la description que j'ai faites vous intéresse, vous pouvez toujours tenter.

Genuielly the coziest game I've played in a long time. For me, someone with major ADHD, it does take me keeping a list on my phone so that I can stay on track, but its such an amazing game, its so much fun, the graphics are amazing, and its just over so much fun.
For me, I love the marriage graphics as well, everytime I got for Harvey, he is the sweetest! I also really like the range of quests and characters, it helps the game be more immersive. Some games I've played have minimal quests and its easy and quick, but this challenges you, it also gives you a big range of time to finish it all. I also love how you can choose what you like to do most, mining, foraging, fishing, farming, completing quests, getting full hearts with everyone, etc.
ANYWAYS, I love the games and totally recommend it to someone who likes cozy games but also likes a bit of range and challenge.

TIPS IF YOU BOUGHT THE GAME: 
- Go to the cindersap forest every Friday and Sunday with money, towards the pink tree/secret forrest there is a cart that can help you finish the community center/help you buy things.
- Check the Stardew Valley WIKI for help, it has info on everything, from Fish to Foraging to Characters.
- If you friend certain characters they will send you things in the mail (I can't remember the characters but look it up on google or youtube)
- Cooking Lady is on the TV every Wednesday (Re-Run) and Sunday. She teaches you new recipes and can really help
- If you're going into the mines, pack high energy foods, you will get lower energy and not be able to finish automatically.
- Giving presents on characters birthdays majorly boosts friendship points
- Finish the community center earlier on, it may not seem important but trust me, it is, it unlocks a lot of important/helpful quests (Like Willy's Boat) and finishing bundles helps a lot (Like with the greenhouse, minecarts, bus to the desert, the quarry, etc.)

While the game seems quite simple at first, it becomes quite vast and complex while still letting you play at your own pace. There is a lot of player agency and nothing is forced onto the player, even farming. despite it being one of its main advertised features. Build a massive farming tycoon, mine rocks and ores to your hearts content, or fish for every penny, you can do whatever you want, whenever. 

You start with simple farming, then work your way to foraging, unlocking new areas that allow mining and dungeon crawling/fighting, to even exploring a whole new custom map near the end of the game. You are consistently hit with new content, new events, and new things to do. While it can be a little daunting or frustrating at times because of no explanation, when you do find secrets or figure out puzzles it's not just rewarding in dopamine, but you typically get unique rewards that make you more efficient.

Stardew Valley is the most comforting and rewarding slice of life game I have played. It looks simple at first but it unfolds into a deep and surprisingly rich experience that keeps pulling me back day after day. The loop is perfect. You start each morning planning your tasks, check the weather, water your crops, feed your animals, and decide whether to head into town, explore the mines, go fishing, or work on upgrades for your farm. Every minute feels purposeful and the small choices you make add up over time in a way that is both relaxing and satisfying.

The world is packed with personality. Pelican Town feels alive, with characters that have routines, birthdays, personal stories, and heart events that make them feel like real neighbors. Building friendships is not just a checklist. Conversations change with the seasons and with your relationship progress, and gift preferences actually make sense once you learn more about each person. Festivals break up the calendar with fun activities and unique rewards, and they give the town a real sense of community.

The progression is excellent. Early on you struggle with energy and time, but small upgrades like better tools, sprinklers, kegs, and barns open up new possibilities. The Community Center bundles give you clear goals and push you to try every part of the game, from foraging and fishing to cooking and animal care. If you prefer a different route you can partner with Joja and rebuild the town a different way. By the time you reach late game you can automate huge parts of your farm, breed animals, create artisan goods, decorate to your taste, and still find reasons to explore.

There is a surprising amount of adventure. The mines and later combat areas add risk and reward, with meaningful gear upgrades, gems, and resources that feed back into crafting and farming. Fishing deserves a special mention. It can be tricky at first, but once it clicks it becomes a relaxing way to spend time, earn money, and fill out collections. The soundtrack ties it all together with gentle themes that change by season and by area, and the pixel art is gorgeous with cozy lighting, weather effects, and the best autumn vibes in any game.

Quality of life is strong. The game teaches you gently and lets you learn by doing. The day timer and energy system encourage planning without ever feeling punishing. Crafting menus, chests, and tool upgrades make routine tasks smooth, and there are lots of small touches that show real care, like being able to reorganize buildings, move sprinklers, or label storage in your own way. Performance is rock solid on both keyboard and controller, and co op is a blast, with shared goals and a nice division of labor between farming, mining, and town errands.

What I love most is the freedom. You can focus on crops and artisan goods, become a fishing expert, design the prettiest farm layout, chase every collection, speed run profits, or take it slow and just enjoy the seasons. There is always a new project within reach. One week I am remodeling the farmhouse and landscaping with paths and fences. The next I am grinding for ore to upgrade sprinklers or trying a new crop rotation. Even after hundreds of days there are secrets, new cut scenes, hidden areas, and rare items to discover.

If I had a gentle warning, it is that time management can be tight early on and the fishing mini game can feel tough until you get a few skill levels and better rods. Stick with it. Those systems start to feel great once you settle in, and the sense of progression is worth it.

Stardew Valley is cozy, generous, and endlessly replay able. It respects your time, rewards your creativity, and makes even the smallest accomplishments feel meaningful. I love this game and I cannot recommend it enough.

A Cozy Escape for Two 

Playing Stardew Valley with my boyfriend has been one of the most unexpectedly wonderful experiences we’ve shared together. What started as a simple farming game turned into hours of laughter, teamwork, and surprisingly heartfelt moments.

From building our dream farm together to running through the mines with him by my side (me usually running from monsters while he bravely fought them off), every moment in the game felt like a little adventure. We picked crops, raised animals, and even argued (lovingly!) over how to organise the chests—somehow, even that was fun.

The best part? Watching our virtual farm grow felt like watching a part of our relationship grow too. We celebrated our first in-game festival together, planted our favourite crops side by side, and even got married in-game (who says digital rings don’t count?).

Stardew Valley has this quiet charm that makes you want to slow down, breathe, and appreciate the little things—and doing that with someone you love makes it even better. It’s more than a game; it’s a cozy little world we built together.

If you’re looking for something sweet to share with your partner, this game is a perfect choice. Just be warned: you might start arguing over whose turn it is to water the crops

Stardew was one of those games that I never got on the initial hype wave for and especially felt daunting after not playing it for so long. It must not have helped that this game was extremely buzzed as being one of the best farm sim/survival/rpg games of all time. Funnily enough, narrowing down what this game is was a lot more challenging than I thought. Initially I just wanted to play a chill farming game however, I quickly found out that this game had a lot more elements to it than met the eye. Fully thought out stat system that tied in with every aspect of the game (friendship levels, farming, fishing, mining, combat, luck, foraging, etc..) which made the game a lot less surface level than I thought. The guy who created this game literally thought of every quality of life thing you could think of, whenever I thought man this is good but I wish it (BLANK) more often than not, there was a way to get that “blank” or upgrade to it. The game was a lot more satisfying than I thought to play with the multiple ways to earn money making it feel like not just having to sit around and wait for crops to grow, as a matter of fact technically you could  almost completely ignore farming if you wanted. The early game of working toward the big goal of restoring the town centre felt very rewarding to finish, and I was scared that I would feel directionless after doing so but there was still SO MUCH MORE to do around the valley with new content being unlocked each year with things like the movie theatre, ginger island, and all the completionist logs you can do. Not to mention everything involved with Mr. Qi felt like the endgame in its own right. The music and artstyle of this game are great, especially for a single dev at the time this is extremely impressive, even more so in combination with the tens of large systems in the game that all work seamlessly and are intertwined. I loved seeing all the different cutscenes and heart events with the villagers and they were all super interesting characters in their own right no two felt the same. Stardew has instantly become one of my favorite games of all time and I am excited to do a replay and do everything differently on a different farm layout when the itch comes back, great game.

Stardew Valley isn’t just a game — it’s a sanctuary. A place where the noise of the world fades away and you’re gently reminded of the quiet beauty in simplicity. It’s not just pixels and code; it’s a feeling. A memory. A second home.

From the moment you arrive in Pelican Town, greeted by its warm, hand-drawn charm and soothing soundtrack, you’re embraced by a world that moves at your pace. Here, time doesn’t chase you — it dances beside you. Whether you’re tilling soil under a spring sunrise, fishing by the gentle murmur of a river, or sharing a quiet evening at the Stardrop Saloon, Stardew Valley invites you to slow down, breathe deeply, and remember what joy feels like.

But beneath the cozy farming life is something far more profound: connection. To the land, to its seasons, to its people. Every villager has a story. Every friendship feels earned. The relationships you build aren’t superficial; they bloom organically, revealing layers of heartache, hope, and humanity. You come to care deeply about these characters — not because the game demands it, but because it inspires it.

And perhaps the most beautiful thing about Stardew Valley is how it reflects you. It doesn’t tell you what kind of life to lead — it hands you the tools and lets you choose. Want to grow a bustling farm, raise animals, and become a tycoon? You can. Want to live quietly, giving gifts to friends and watching the seasons change? You can. Want to explore mines and fight monsters under the moonlight? You can do that too. There is no right path — only your path.

ConcernedApe has never charged for an update or DLC, and they listens to the community providing a wonderful game years after it's been released. 

~Things I love about the game~

- Farming/ animal raising
- NPC's personality and interactions
- The simple but bright style of the game
- The endless ways the game can be replayed. With different routes and different story potential.
- Diverse game play. You can be a farmer or a miner or fisher! You have the choice of how to play and make money.
- The Addition of FREE updates like: Ginger Island, desert festival, all of 1.6 update really! Years after the game has released  it's still loved and cared for by a ConcernedApe and a small team which is incredible for an indie game.
- The ability to decorate and make the town and your farm unique.
- The ease to mod and make the game even more unique! 

~Things I dislike~
- Clint. [spoiler] He's so weird towards Emily (creepy Niceguy™)  and during Emily's 8th heart event he says "congrats' like Emily is a prize to win rather than a person. Also even after marriage to Emily his dialogue towards her and his crush makes me dislike him further. [/spoiler] If he has one hater it's me. If he has 0 haters I have died.
- The lack of change of dialogue and gifts after marriage or events take place. [spoiler]Shane's liking being gifted alcohol after all his events and growth makes me upset. I also dislike how messy his spouse room is :/ lemme clean it.  [/spoiler]
- The fishing game - I suck at the minigame so this is a bias dislike XD
- Combat can suck. I'd like to feel more diverse towards weapon choice other than infinity weapons.  Allow some weapons to be upgraded to have higher damage or something? I dunno.
- The lack of content with your own children. Some dialogue or scenes with them would be lovely or them going to school with Jaz and Vincent. 


Overall: This game is worth every cent and a genuine delight to play. I really could not suggest it more if story and farming games are your thing!  Thank you ConcernedApe <3

Stardew Valley is the best game I've played in a very long time. I haven't dabbled in any mods yet, but the vanilla OG game gives so much to explore and do and easily has 100+ hours of extremely engaging content. 

[b]FULL DISCLOSURE:[/b] I did not expect to love this game. I thought it was going to be a mediocre farming sim with light RPG elements with maybe 7 hours worth of content I'd somewhat enjoy. Quite honestly, I think that's why many people are hesitant on playing this game. However, not only are the farming and RPG elements very engaging, but other elements such as mining, fishing, and completing quests are just as well thought out. I've had multiple days where I completely lose track of time from getting so immersed in Stardew. The game is also just made really well, which is so rare from most games these days. The art, sound design, style, and lore are all very top notch.  

Stardew is not without it's flaws. The first 2-3 hours of playtime DRAGS because of your lack of energy. The first spring and summer was very unproductive for me because of how limiting your starting energy is. However, the slow start almost works in Stardew's favor. When I finally began to get upgrades, the game became a lot more fun, largely because I could do so much more in one day. My other major gripe with Stardew is how shallow marriage is in its current state. I feel like after 10, and especially after 14 hearts, I feel like I cycle between the same 10 dialogues on a daily basis. I will say that this is a really minor gripe, but I would love to see a bit more expansion of marriage in the base game. 

Regardless, Stardew is one of the best games I've ever played. Easily some of the best $15 I ever spent. ConcernedApe, THANK YOU for making this masterpiece!

I've only played Stardew Valley for a couple of hours, and it's already been a journey! The game is incredibly charming, but I'm clearly a natural disaster when it comes to farming life. My first night, I lost track of time, got caught in the rain, and just... passed out right there on the ground. The next morning, I got a letter informing me that "unconsciousness is dangerous" and a bill for the emergency services that found me! I didn't even know that was possible. On day two, I was determined to clear the land around my house. I got a little too enthusiastic with my axe, chopped one too many trees, and collapsed from exhaustion right on my own doorstep. Cue another letter and another medical bill. My farmer is a liability, and I've earned more debt at this point. Despite my character's apparent death wish, I'm having a blast. The fact that the game has these funny, forgiving consequences for failure makes it feel alive and lighthearted. I'm learning to manage my energy and time, and the loop of "work, nearly die, get a bill, repeat" is weirdly addictive. It's a cozy, funny, and surprisingly deep game, even if my bank account in Pelican Town is already in the red. Can't wait to see what other trouble I can get into lol!

As someone who usually plays games like DOOM, ULTRAKILL, and The Binding of Isaac, I never thought a farming game would appeal to me, but I was completely wrong.

Stardew Valley is so much more than just farming. There’s an incredible amount of variety, and it genuinely makes me feel happy when I play. The characters are a huge part of that. Each one has their own personality, dialogue, and routines, which makes the town feel alive instead of lifeless like most NPCs in other games.

What really surprised me is how much it feels like a life simulator. Every in-game day has purpose. One day you might spend time in the mines, another fishing, doing farm work, completing quests, or attending festivals. There’s always something to do, and the constant decision-making makes each day feel meaningful.

I also love how the characters don’t just stand around waiting for you. They have their own schedules, hobbies, and lives, which makes the world feel real.

I haven’t fully completed the game yet, but I’ve played enough to confidently say that I love it. This game completely changed my expectations of what a “farming game” could be.

Easily one of my favourite games of all time... as a "cozy" game, I can understand why people might get a bit stressed out by playing it compared to some of the older games in the genre (Harvest Moon etc.). The community, while helpful at times, can definitely add to that stress because you'll see all sorts of crazy/efficient builds and farms. I strongly suggest you just ignore all of that, all the Youtube guides etc. and just play the game at your own pace. Use the wiki if you have to, especially if you're curious about what gifts people like, or what fish are only available during certain conditions. Otherwise... don't sweat it. Don't worry about how much someone else did in Year 1. Don't worry about how nicely organized someone's chests or rooms are, how cool their paths look, or what's the "best" farm layout... just play it however you want. After you've sunk a few dozen hours in, THEN start looking for ways to improve if that's truly your goal. Avoid mods at the beginning too... it's a great game in it's own right and deserves to be played "as is" before you start experimenting.

NICE

The Ultimate Escape from Reality

The Good
Pure Therapeutic Freedom: There is no rush, no pressure, and no game-over screen. You can spend your days farming, fishing, mining, foraging, or doing absolutely nothing at all.

Masterpiece Soundtrack: The music dynamically shifts with the seasons, perfectly capturing the cozy, melancholic, and joyful vibes of rural life.

Deep Town Lore: The residents of Pelican Town feel like real people with complex lives, struggles, and personal growth as you build relationships with them.

Endless Progression: Just when you think you've seen it all, the game opens up with deep-sea fishing, desert exploration, casino gambling, and entire new islands to unlock.

Flawless Multi-player: Sharing a farm with friends splits the labor and quadruples the chaotic fun of trying to optimize your ancient fruit wine empire.

Developer Love: ConcernedApe (the solo developer) has provided massive, game-changing free updates for a decade, refusing to ever charge for DLC.

The Bad
The "One More Day" Addiction: You will say "I'll just play one more day" at 11:00 PM, and suddenly the real-life sun is rising outside your window.

Inventory Management: Early game backpack space is painfully small, forcing you to constantly choose what valuable loot to throw away.

Verdict: 10 / 10

Stardew Valley was the catalyst for the indie cozy game trend, and it remains the best of its genre 9 years after, due to its: consistent updates, large community, and frequent developer interaction.

One of the game's biggest strengths however, is how it builds upon the ideas of it's inspiration Harvest Moon and improves them, while developing its own ideas; all of this is executed with many layers of polish, and it all flourishes with detail and mechanical depth. All of this is complimented by the incredibly low system requirements, allowing anyone on any piece of hardware to enjoy Stardew Valley.

The game allows you to play however you want, there's no wrong way to play the game. You can develop your farm, harvesting more crops and creating more produce, or start a family with one of the 12 bachelors and bachelorettes. You could fish by the river and sell tons of fish, or explore caverns filled with monsters and loot. The list is near endless, and I have barely experienced any of it.

It's one of the highest-selling, and highest rated, games on Steam for a good reason. It's absolutely worth every penny, and I'd pay so much more for it. Buy Stardew Valley, now. I am not asking.

Never goes super in depth with its mechanics or balances them well. Not even the start feels that balanced. But it does enough with what it has to keep you playing. It definitely does tickle your bone in your body that likes to explore from time to time (lest you'll probably have to wiki-dive for questions you have).

The highlight of the game isn't really the farming. Everything related to crops or animals isn't that rewarding besides easy money. There's maybe a few days of unique content that you'll likely care about, everything else is intermittent. The other skills will probably interest you more if you want more active gameplay.

Many say to not do a modded playthrough the first time but I would say honestly give it a shot if the game doesn't interest you in some aspects. I've had way much more fun with faster animations + marriage mod (the marriage candidate pool is limited and the gameplay loop is a bit slow, especially when trying to go through all its content). Stardew Valley is honestly one of those games that seems dead simple on the surface, but somehow just sticks with you. I remember booting it up for the first time with basically no expectations - more out of curiosity than anything - and it didn’t hit me all at once. It’s not loud, it’s not flashy, it doesn’t try to grab you straight away. It sort of creeps up on you instead.. and then suddenly you realise you’ve been thinking about it even when you’re not playing.

You start off with this run-down farm, barely any tools, no clue what you’re doing, and somehow that’s exactly the point. There’s no pressure, no “right way” to play, no constant feeling that you’re falling behind. You can take things at your own pace, mess things up, waste entire days doing basically nothing - and the game just lets you. It’s got that quiet “do whatever you fancy” energy, which you don’t really get in a lot of games anymore.

After a bit, you fall into this routine without even noticing. Wake up, sort your crops, wander into town, have a quick chat with someone, maybe do a bit of fishing or head into the mines and it all starts to feel like your own little life. It sounds repetitive, but it’s not in a boring way - it’s the kind of routine that actually feels calming. Even the smallest bit of progress feels weirdly rewarding.

What surprised me the most is how attached you get. To the place, the people, the whole vibe of it. The villagers aren’t just background characters, they’ve all got their own stories, their own issues, and they feel… real, in a way. You end up caring more than you expect, like they’re not just NPCs but actual people you sort of know.

The graphics are pixelated, yeah, but in that really warm, nostalgic way that just works. Everything feels soft and cosy, like a memory you didn’t realise you missed. And the music.. there are moments where it’s so calm you just end up standing there doing nothing, just listening.

And probably the best part - there’s no pressure. In a world where most games are constantly pushing you to do more, faster, better… this one just lets you exist. You can spend a whole day fishing, the next in the mines, the next just wandering about doing absolutely nothing and it still feels right.

It’s not for everyone if you’re after constant action and chaos, you’ll probably get bored. But if you want something calm, cosy, and a bit of an escape from everything, it’s actually hard to beat.

And honestly, one little tip from me if you’re just starting out - don’t stress about playing it “right”, but at the same time do yourself a favour and check a few tips on YouTube!! Not in a sweaty, try-hard way, just casually. There are so many little things the game barely explains, and you don’t even realise you’re doing something the hard way until it’s way too late. I swear, I found out some basic stuff embarrassingly late and just sat there like.. right, could’ve saved myself HOURS (╥﹏╥)

It’s more about making your life easier than anything. Like small things — how to organise your farm, what’s actually worth upgrading first, where to spend your gold early on — it just makes everything feel smoother and way less overwhelming. Especially at the start when you’re low on energy, broke, and slightly confused most of the time.

And also… SV with mods is a whole different story. Like I’m not even exaggerating - it goes from “this is such a nice cosy game” to “I live here now”. You can add new characters, new areas, extra storylines, loads of quality-of-life stuff… even just small visual mods can change the whole vibe. It starts feeling really personal, like your own little version of the game.

It’s that kind of cosy where you sit down thinking you’ll play for a bit, and next thing you know it’s late, you’re still there, fully invested in your crops, your relationships, your little routines it’s just comfort. Proper cosy, no stress, just vibes.

If you’ve been feeling stressed, having a rough time, or just a bit overwhelmed and you’re looking for something to properly calm your head down, this is honestly the perfect game. Like seriously this game is like a little reset button for your brain. Everything in it is slow, peaceful, and pressure-free, so it’s really easy to just switch off from all the chaos going on outside the game. Especially if you’ve got music on in the background,some chill playlist or just anything soft the vibe becomes unbeatable. Everything just blends together and it lowkey feels like you’re actually unwinding properly, not just playing a game.

Stardew Valley – A Game That Never Truly Ends

Stardew Valley is not just a farming game; it’s a peaceful escape, a second life, and one of the most beautifully designed indie games ever created. At first glance, it may look simple, but the depth hidden beneath its pixel art is absolutely incredible.

I’ve played over 100+ hours, and even after all that time, I still haven’t fully completed the story — and that’s the magic of Stardew Valley. The game never rushes you. It lets you play at your own pace, whether you want to farm, fish, mine, build relationships, or simply enjoy the calm atmosphere of Pelican Town.

Every villager feels alive, with their own personalities, struggles, and stories that slowly unfold over time. Building relationships isn’t just about gifting items — it’s about understanding people, their pasts, and their emotions. This makes the world feel deeply personal and real.

The gameplay loop is incredibly relaxing yet addictive. One more day turns into one more season, and before you realize it, hours have passed. There’s always something new to discover — hidden events, secrets, festivals, upgrades, and long-term goals that keep pulling you back in.

What truly makes Stardew Valley special is how it makes you feel. It’s calming without being boring, deep without being overwhelming, and emotional without forcing drama. Even after 100+ hours, the fact that the story still isn’t fully complete shows just how much content and heart this game has.

Stardew Valley isn’t about finishing everything quickly — it’s about enjoying the journey. And that journey feels endless in the best way possible.

I miiiiiiight have gotten slightly addicted to this game, but in my defense, it's tons of fun. The graphics are incredible, the music rocks, and the open world lets you go at your own pace. You can farm crops as well as raise animals (I recently got the Deluxe Barn and a sheep let's go); depending on how you play and what you want to accomplish, there isn't a "wrong" way to go about playing the game.

There are several advancements that keep you from getting bored. Without getting into spoilers, you can mine in the caves, develop friendships and romance, forage for wild plants, and even fish. (I am terrible at the fishing minigame, but maybe you won't be!) There's also the option to forage around in trashcans if you wish to do a bit of trolling.

There's a loose overarching story, but day-to-day life consists of working on your farm, mining, etc. It definitely lives up to its cozy reputation, but there are some deeper elements thrown in there such as an evil corporation and more somber elements in some characters' arcs. You're not being railroaded into liking a certain character or doing a certain thing on a certain day (other than celebrating festivals, but you technically don't HAVE to go to those). So yeah, I'd say this game is pretty lit.

I picked this game up originally back in, like, 2018 or 19 or whatever, and thought it was pretty awesome save for the terrible combat.

Fast forward to now, and it's gotten even better, with so many quality of life improvements and extra content that you'd be insane not to capitalize on the sheer bang for your buck. Except for the combat.

Some games will give you the power fantasy of carving through demons, some will have you leading armies and out-smarting your enemies. This game gives you the ultimate power fantasy for a man in 2025: living off the land with a beautiful wife and kids. And the only demons you're fighting off are A) the evil Amazon stand-in and B) the stupid effing flying enemies that drag the game to a halt as you stand there knocking them away and waiting for them to bounce back like the slowest, most boring game of paddle ball in the universe. Combat sucks.

There'll inevitably be that time where you realize that you're 90% done with the game, even if that 10% will take a hefty while to achieve, and that'll drag down your mood. But it'll take you _quite_ a while to get there, and it's all worth it for that sense of accomplishment. And if the problem is, "Aw, I was hoping there'd be just a *little* bit more," then I'd say, after forty-something hours, that's a freakin' accomplishment.

If I had only _one_ piece of feedback...we could *maybe* have enemies die in less than twenty hits. Maybe. Definitely. Absolutely. Enemies shouldn't take nearly twenty hits to kill with the highest-level sword in the game. We ain't here for the paddle ball, Eric - we're here for the *literally everything else*. The likable npcs, the cute gals, the mysteries, and the soil. And fishing, sometimes. When I'm in the mood. I'm not often in the mood. But we're getting off track.

This game has a lot of content and it took me a long time to beat.  When I say "beat," I mean "perfect."  Because the only way to really beat the game is to 100% it, which is very time-consuming.

There's not really much of a story except for at the beginning.  Otherwise, you basically just build up your life, family, friends and town.  There are really only two mutually exclusive choices to make, but they mostly lead to similar outcomes, and the rewards are different.

When starting the game, you can choose what kind of farm you want between a regular farm, beach farm, a forage farm, a farm with monsters, etc.  The goal is still the same; sow, harvest, get paid.

I lost track of how many quests there were, mostly because a lot of them repeat.  If I were to summarize it into different parts, I'd limit it to the following:  Farming, mining, relationships and community.

Farming is what you would think; grow crops, build coops and stables, care for animals, produce artisan goods, craft stuff, cook dishes, etc.

Mining is more of the adventurous and combative part of the game where you explore the floors of mines, fight enemies, find rare resources and artifacts, forge, find and upgrade weapons, etc.

Relationships involve the local and non-local citizens.  Talking to them, gifting them things they like or completing quests for them increase your relationship.  In contrast, saying mean things, hitting trashcans in front of them, or gifting them things they don't like will decrease your relationship.  There are events that happen at various times and places once you've reached a certain relationship threshold with a particular person and it reveals a little more depth to their lives and develops their character further.  There are bachelors and bachelorettes that can be romanced and eventually married, after which they move in with you, enabling you to have/adopt up to 2 children.  Some of this cannot be done until you've upgraded your house sufficiently.  There are a number of characters that are either already married or cannot otherwise be romanced.  There are mods that can change this, FYI.  I didn't use any of them, for the record.

The community-related part of the game involves developments that improve things around town, like fixing buses, boats or bridges that lead to new places, fixing the greenhouse on your property for indoor farming, removing rocks so that ore and minerals flow through the town's water, etc.  This is the part where there are two mutually exclusive ways to go about it.  The developer has made it very apparent that one of these ways is their preferred way, and is a lot more in-depth and time-consuming in nature.  The other way is more efficient, but is made to feel more empty in the end.  Some of the new places revealed by these developments are beyond the local town, and there are different caves, mines, farms, people and quests to work with.  Like I said, this game has a lot of content.

I can see why so many people like this game.  I'd say the unfortunate part for me was that I got overwhelmed at one point and had to put it down.  I came back a few years later to complete it.  It's difficult to do this, however, because I had to remember how everything worked and how I left things originally. 

Anyway, I think most adventure gamers, or people who like games such as Terraria or Minecraft would enjoy this game a lot.

This game was on my ignore list for almost a decade now, because judging by the screenshots I assumed that it was a game primarily targeted at children with presumably little content for mature audiences. I only recently stumbled upon this game while I was browsing for cozy/relaxing games to play after a stressful day at work and I have to say that I am really glad that I gave it a try, because it is definitely one of the best cozy/relaxing games that I have ever played.

Stardew Valley really stands out in two ways: First, this game is not only about farming, but it also contains other mechanics that you can spend your time on, namely foraging, fishing, mining as well as various activities based around the social contacts to NPCs as well as festivals of the village. While this by itself is not unique and other similar games also offer different activities, Stardew Valley manages to provide a perfect balance between these activities in the sense that I have never felt bored by these activities in this game, because firstly the relatively short length of a single day (about 15 minutes real-time) prevents you from sticking too long in a single activity loop, and secondly the activities feel sufficiently different from each other that they provide a nice variety, although it's hard for me to find the right words to describe what I mean (being a non-native English speaker).

The second part that makes this game so nice and relaxing to play is that there is pretty much no way to screw up: Your avatar cannot die, your plants won't die if you don't water them, your animals won't starve if you don't feed them, there is no way to go bankrupt or to screw up social relations too badly -- the worst thing that could happen is that you lose some money if you get knocked out or that your plants/animals don't grow and don't produce goods while you're neglecting them. Most other similar games try to put some sort of pressure by penalizing you if you don't take care of your characters or other NPC's basic needs, which then reduces the "cozyness" of the game by introducing a stress factor.

So, in short: if you're looking for a game to relax, then Stardew Valley is an absolute unit. I do recommend reading/watching a "First Steps in Stardew Valley" guide or video before starting your first playthrough, because the game gives you relatively little information on how to start.

Stardew Valley is a simple game on the surface, but somehow it holds a quiet kind of magic—the kind that feels stronger when you’re not playing alone. I started the farm for myself, but it became something much bigger once my friends joined me. We watered crops half-asleep at dawn, sprinted into the mines together, got lost in the forest at night, and laughed over the most ridiculous mistakes. None of it was dramatic, yet every moment felt warm.

What Stardew teaches you is that happiness is often found in routine—planting seeds, tending animals, watching the seasons change—but the joy doubles when someone shares those small moments with you. When we built our first barn together, or sat by the beach during the in-game summer festival, it didn’t feel like pixels. It felt like a memory.

The game never pushes you. It simply gives you a place to breathe, to slow down, and to appreciate the people beside you—both on the farm and in real life. Stardew Valley isn’t just relaxing; it’s a reminder that comfort can be grown, just like a crop, as long as you have good friends to grow it with.

So I bought Stardew Valley thinking I'd relax for an hour.
That was January 2026.
I have no idea what year it is anymore.
The game starts innocently enough. You inherit a charming little farm, meet friendly townsfolk, pet some chickens, and think, "I'll just water my crops and then go to bed."
That, my friends, was the first lie.
Every in-game day ends with:
"Okay, just one more day."
Then suddenly you're optimizing sprinkler layouts like you're managing a Fortune 500 company. You're carrying seventeen different crops, twelve jars of mayonnaise, three mysterious artifacts, a fish that only appears every third Tuesday during a thunderstorm at exactly 6:40 PM while Mercury is in retrograde, and somehow you're still late to Pierre's before he closes.
Meanwhile, real life has completely fallen apart.
My laundry has become an archaeological dig site.
My dishes have formed diplomatic relations with the mold.
My family checks on me by sliding food under the door like I'm a dangerous zoo animal.
I haven't seen the sun in so long that I flinched when Windows switched to light mode.
Inside Stardew, however?
Millionaire.
Married.
Two kids. (I think I have 4 IRL, but I honestly can't remember)
An ancient wine empire.
A fully automated farm that NASA would be jealous of.
Best friends with an actual wizard.
Saved the community.
Own an island resort.
Outside the game?
I celebrated my birthday because my Steam friends wished me happy birthday before my actual family remembered.
The worst part is how Stardew rewires your brain.
I'll walk outside and see a dandelion and instinctively think:
"Nice. That's 40g."
It starts raining and my first thought isn't "I should grab an umbrella."
It's:
"Sweet. I don't have to water the crops."
Then reality hits...
I don't HAVE crops.
I have a mortgage.
The soundtrack has become my internal monologue.
I hear birds chirping and immediately wonder where Linus is hiding.
Someone mentions mayonnaise and I instinctively calculate artisan profit margins.
At this point I'm convinced ConcernedApe didn't make a farming simulator.
He made the most polite hostage situation ever created.
No explosions.
No violence. (Well except for serpants flying at your face at mach 286.
No dragons threatening the kingdom.
Just one tiny little sentence that has consumed thousands of hours of my life:
"One more day."
Final Verdict:
Graphics: Cozy enough to erase responsibilities. ★★★★★
Gameplay: Accidentally invents time travel. ★★★★★
Difficulty: Explaining why it's suddenly 3:47 AM. ★★★★★
Impact on Social Life: "Your friends have forgotten what you look like." ★★★★★
Would I recommend it?
Absolutely.
Would I warn people first?
Also absolutely.
Because Stardew Valley isn't a game...
It's a legally purchased black hole where weekends, responsibilities, and entire seasons disappear without a trace.
Now if you'll excuse me...
I just need to harvest one more crop.
...and that's definitely where I'll stop.

there are several fun mechanics in Stardew that keep it feeling dynamic. The farming, fishing, mining/combat, helping the neighbors foraging/exploring, they all work together well to keep things moving along. You can choose a relaxed or more intense playthrough by choosing a couple or all of the challenges. I've chosen to focus on a few of those things in my first playthrough where as my wife plays to beat her perfection record. Choosing the perfection route and completing all the tasks and upgrades is not for the casual player though. The day/night and season cycles become more stressful the more challenges you choose. The feeling of accomplishing your goal for the day is really satisfying.

Some of the controls could be a bit better. I often pick something up and its in my hands when I don't want it there. Half the time I end up eating something I didn't want to or giving something to someone that negatively affects friendship levels. The selection box shouldn't stay on an empty inventory spot. The combat could be a bit more fluid if the weapons didn't take so long to swing before you could move again. It makes combat very sticky and inflexible. There doesn't seem to be a way to beat the game unless you're set your own time limit or goal such as completing all the quests given by townsfolk or perfection. I guess that's another thing to choose in the game. I still haven't decided what that is. Overall its a well made game with a lot of fun for those that enjoy the survival, crafter, adventure style.

Its very easy to hyperfixate on one specific thing, and neglect other things in pursuit of it. But often, this makes your life way harder in the long run. Sure, you can spend all day, every day, manually watering calculated plots of exactly 248 cranberry bushes, because the internet told you cranberries were a fast way to make money. But you will hate it. And you will miss out on so much. Do a little bit of everything instead, and youll find it way less stressful to keep up. Plant 5 cranberry bushes instead, and stop to enjoy other things some more. You end up making the same amount of progress either way.

It immediately drew me in with its simple mechanics and complex characters. (I say simple mechanics because I have played many survival games in the past, including Rust, Sons of the forest, and seven days to die. I am not saying this game is too basic by any means)  I was genuinely surprised by how in depth everything was. I found myself wanting to learn more about the characters and the world around them. I could relate to many of them. Harvey and Shane to be more specific. The farm became more of a farm to me. It became something I was actively building, coexisting with the real life I was trying to rebuild. I know there are dozens of reviews like mine, and I’m being completely honest when I say this game changed my life. It changed my perspective. It gave me hope. It made me want to write  and draw again. (Fanfics and fanart) Something that I had been missing and no longer had energy for, from being so burnt out from everything that was happening to me. Playing stardew valley between job applications and interviews helped me stay positive and have something to look forward to when things didn’t go as planned. I eventually did end up getting a job, and things did start working out. It took time. And while I am still working towards ‘Perfection’ in the game, I am also learning that my own life doesn’t have to be perfect, it just has to be lived.
Thank you ConcernedApe for helping an anxious depressed fellow find his motivation to create again. Follow your passion. Things will get better. There is always someone out there who cares. The world is a better place with you in it.

Your first week in game will be slow - meeting villagers, getting to know the different game mechanics, swearing that you will fish as little as possible in this game (yet once you figure it out you'll miss the Stardew fishing in every other game you play) and chopping lots of trees to build a few storage chests. 

But soon after you'll have more things to do than you know what to do with (hint: pick one activity per day, pack lots of food, and you'll be fine) and occasionally dying in the mines or passing out from exhaustion. But it's part of the fun. 

You will laugh and cry with the villagers stories, you'll discover secrets that change your first impressions of people, and you'll be deep-diving in the wiki to optimize your time and farm layout. 

Also, this game continues to get major updates 10 years after release, which is insane - and a testament to how much love and dedication ConcernedApe puts into his work.

“Why I Stole Caroline from Pierre” – A Stardew Valley Love Story 

When I first arrived in Pelican Town, all I wanted was peace. I was tired of the noise of the city, the endless grind, the feeling that life was passing me by one cubicle at a time. I came here to find something simple: dirt under my nails, sun on my face, and maybe, if the stars were kind, a few friendly faces.

I didn’t expect her.

The first time I stepped into Pierre’s General Store, I was just looking for parsnip seeds. But when I saw Caroline, everything else faded. Her laughter filled the room like sunlight through dusty windows, her green hair catching the glow of the afternoon light. She smiled politely, asked how the farm was going, and I forgot how to speak for a moment. I told myself it was nothing, a harmless crush on a friendly villager.

But days turned into weeks, and soon I was visiting the store every morning. Pierre would brag about his prices while I pretended to browse, sneaking glances toward the sunroom where Caroline sipped tea and read quietly. Sometimes she would look up and smile, and the world would stop for a heartbeat.

She loved the simple things: tea, fresh flowers, the sound of the rain on the roof. I started bringing her little gifts, a daffodil from my field, a cup of green tea I brewed myself, a diamond when my mine trips were lucky. She always thanked me softly, her voice like spring wind. I told myself it was innocent. It wasn’t.

The town began to whisper. Pierre grew colder. But I couldn’t stop. When she invited me to share tea with her one morning, I knew I was lost. The scent of jasmine filled the air as she spoke about her dreams, how she once wanted to travel, to see the world beyond Pelican Town, before life settled her into routine. “Sometimes,” she said, “I feel like my heart belongs to another season.”

That was the moment. The one where everything changed.

It wasn’t sudden; love rarely is. It grows slowly, like the crops we tend, roots deepening quietly beneath the surface. Every glance, every conversation, every shared silence made it harder to ignore. I wasn’t just the farmer anymore. I was the person who reminded her what it felt like to dream.

Pierre tried to fight it. He slashed prices, gave me dirty looks at festivals, and once, I swear, sold me defective fertilizer out of spite. But love doesn’t need discounts. It needs honesty, patience, and the courage to follow your heart even when it leads somewhere you shouldn’t go.

The night she came to my farmhouse, the rain was pouring. She stood at my door, soaked but smiling, eyes shining with something I had never seen before. “I can’t pretend anymore,” she said. “I’ve lived my whole life for others. I want to live for myself now. With you.”

That’s how it began, not with fireworks, but with quiet truth.

Now, years later, Caroline and I live together on the farm. She tends to her tea saplings in the mornings while I work the fields. In the evenings, we sit by the fire, sipping wine made from our first harvest of ancient fruit, listening to the soft hum of crickets outside. Our two children chase fireflies by the pond, their laughter echoing through the valley. Sometimes, when I see her watching them with that gentle smile, I realize that this life is everything we ever wanted.

Pierre still runs the General Store. We visit him sometimes. It’s awkward, but there’s peace between us now. Maybe he understands. Maybe he always did. After all, the heart isn’t a store. You can’t own it, you can’t stock it, you can’t sell it. You can only nurture it, and hope it blooms.

And Caroline? She’s still the same, kind, warm, and a little mischievous. Every spring, she plants new flowers around our home, and every year, the valley seems just a little brighter.

I came to Stardew Valley to escape the noise of the world. I found love instead.

Es, sin duda, uno de los mejores juegos de granja jamás creados. Tiene un encanto difícil de explicar: una combinación perfecta entre jugabilidad relajante, personajes entrañables y una banda sonora que se queda contigo. Las actualizaciones constantes han mejorado muchísimo la experiencia sin perder su esencia original.

Aunque todavía hay algunos pequeños detalles de calidad de vida (UX) que podrían mejorar, el contenido actual es más que suficiente. Es un juego que marcó época, que inspiró a muchos otros indies, y que sigue tan vigente como el primer día.

Let me start by saying that Stardew Valley has firmly placed itself in the Top 3 of my favorite games of all time. I do take breaks from time to time, but I ALWAYS end up coming back to start a new farm and try out something I haven't done before in other playthroughs.
I'll start out by going over some dislikes I have, all be it very few, then we can move on to the good stuff.

Dislikes:

1. Clint. Look I know it's a meme to hate on this guy, but it does come from reason. There is something about his personality that just comes across, to me, as a whiney man baby, that just doesn't sit right with me. His constant obsession with Emily, as an adult, is weird. Its like an elementary school kid having a crush, as an adult its just weird. Then, what is this guy's hours. He closes at 4pm. What else does he have to do all day? He literally does nothing besides a blacksmith, which is a huge part of the game, yet this dude closes at 4pm. 
2. Harvey/The Clinic. I understand the need for this location from a gameplay perspective and a in-world perspective, but same issue as Clint but worse....what on earth are these hours. I feel like I NEVER interact with the clinic yet Harvey AND Maru work there. Every time I ever see Harvey he's just standing around not even in the clinic and Maru isn't even behind the desk 50% of the time. On top of that its only open from like 11am-3pm. Why? It doesn't help that Harvey as a character is so dull and boring. I wish there was more of a purpose for The Clinic as a whole.
3. Some of the Farm choices. This is a very small nitpick, but some of the farm types I find to be confusing on why I would ever choose them. Hilltop is significantly smaller than any other farm in map size but also WAY less space to even build or farm in. Its a cool idea for a farm, I just wish it had more room to breathe. The Wilderness farm is also a weird one to me, mostly because there's an option in game to turn on or off Monster Spawns on any Farm type.

Likes:

1. The Progression. I've never played a game with a progression system as satisfying. Throughout all the types of skills, the slow burn of tiering up weapons and gaining XP in each skill to become more efficient, I don't know its just super satisfying. 
2. The Characters(as a whole). The sheer amount of character lore and growth and amount of interactions and dialogue, its stunning someone came up with all of this and has it all work together so well. I will never begin to understand the Dark Magic that Concerned Ape was able to conjure to map out this many NPC's individual schedules that are ALL dependent on what season, character progression, weather, etc. Its emaculate. 
3. The Art style. This game is the king of 2D Pixel Art. Everything about the way this game looks is just iconic. As a Pixel Artist myself, its so fun to see all the ways things are made to look like, from the shaping to the shading, etc.
4. Gameplay Variety. A lot of the time with games like this, players are mostly locked into a certain playstyle. However, with Stardew, you can be a casual gamer who's just trying to play the game as it comes. You could be an absolute chad and minmax the entire game. You can even play it entirely as a dating sim game with the NPCs. There's so many ways to play the game, which add to its replayability.

Conclusion(for now):

As of the time of this review, I have admittedly, not had the ability to explore much of Ginger Island, so I can not speak on that edition to the game. However I have watched my wife play through a lot of it, and I can say its impressive how much extra has been added to the point it feels like a whole seperate game that most companies would be charging full price for, and its just a free update. 

Overall, I think any type of gamer or even non-gamer, should give this game a try. I have recommended this game to a bunch of people over the years, that come from different walks of life, and I have yet to find someone who didn't have a blast playing this game in whatever capacity they had played it. 

If you have EVER considered trying the game, just get it. Don't wait for a sale or anything, its worth every bit of the cost and more. We still get FREE major content updates. Just do yourself a favorite and join the millions of us who have forever made a special place in their soul for this game. 
9.9/10-Clint made the -0.1, sorry.

Now, for those who like reading long ass reviews [b] (no spoilers) [/b] :
Be me in 2017. Freshly in university and meeting other big gaming fans. So far, I have only really played Pokémon or other creature collector games, or straight up JRPGs like Dragon Quest. I have never really played Farming Sims, or Simulators over all, maybe a bit Sims and Animal Crossing New World for the DS when I was very young
Then my friend recommends me this game for the Switch, that she just hasn't been able to put down. Stardew Valley.
I like the art style but I am not really convinced. This isn't the type of game I usually play. But I trusted her and bought the game for my Switch (at the time it even was on sale and costed like...5€ or smth?). 
Skip forward a whole week and there I am sitting in my lecture, not being able to put down my Switch and completely focusing on my farm.

Stardew Valley started my love for farming simulators. Here on Steam I have roughly 200h (at the point of this review) and on my Switch around 150h.
In the meantime I have checked out a whole lot of different Cozy Farming Sims but I always come back to Stardew. The artstyle, the music and the gameplay overall just keep me hooked and even 9 years later, I will always recommend this game to someone, who never heard of it or is hesitant to play it.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ BUGS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
In the day and age, were buggy and unplayable games come out, this game never disappoints. In my whole 9 years, I have never encountered a game breaking bug, neither on Switch, nor here on PC. I am sure I have seen a few smaller bugs here and there but I honestly can't remember.
Also, whenever a new Update comes out, it will be fully functional and playable. No unplayable state or making existing systems worse. It is sad that this is something that needs to be mentioned nowadays but it is part of why I still love this game to this day.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PC REQUIREMENTS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
This game runs on the biggest potato PCs and shouldn't cause any major issues or frame drops. My beefy PC nowadays can run the game without a sweat and roughly 8 years ago, when I bought Stardew Valley for my PC back then, that wouldn't be really able to run a lot of modern games, I never experienced any stutters.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PRICE & PLAYTIME ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
In my personal opinion, the 14€ for this game are more than worth it. If you are big into Farming Sims, you will easily reach over 100 hours (or 1000), so 14€ for a one time purchase? No brainer. In case you don't have enough money, the game does go on Sale pretty often and I think you can easily get it for half the price or less.
And in the case that you will get bored and think that there should be more content? Just look into the Modding Community and your playtime will easily double or triple, OR there are so many stupid challenges people have done over the years, that maybe something tickles your fancy


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ AUDIO ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
Absolutely beautiful pieces. I have studied for various exams just listening to the soundtrack and it's just such a comfy vibe. Music always fits the season/situation, except maybe the mines but I still like the calmer vibe of the songs in there, it makes the mine runs just a nice experience.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GRAPHICS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
Nice pixel art style that has captured my heart. Personally I really love the villager portraits, they way no one looks the same and isn't just straight up perfect. Filled with enough details but also a very unique and charming fantastical look.


[h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GAMEPLAY ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3]
The gameplay. The bread and butter of every cozy farming sim.
The loop is fairly simple. You wake up at 6am and can do whatever you want until preferably 12am, or at the latest 2am.
You can fish, grow veggies, take care of your farm animal, clean up your farm, hang out with the villagers, do a mine run or just run around the village exploring. There are a lot of small details and other things you can do but I don't want to spoil these, since I think that they will be a nice and pleasant surprise. Just know, that the game can go deeper than you may think at first.
Really, you can play the game however you want and in the speed you want.
If you are a min-maxer, there are tons of ways on how to optimize your farm and get a lot of money as quickly as possible.
If you just want to vibe, make your farm look pretty and take it easy, you can also just do that.

There are a bunch of customization features available and if you look up farms online, you can see how many possibilities there are to make your farm and house look absolutely stunning.

The overarching story isn't really a lot of content and you will see it all during a normal run normally. Where most of the story is, is in the heart events. Personally I think every villager is worth getting to max hearts, because everyone is nice and charming, having their own unique quirks (except maybe one but oh well).
Still there are certain goals that you can work towards but you aren't forced to do it. Over the years, more and more goals got added and they will help you to get deeper into certain parts of the gameplay features.

Difficulty wise I would say, that it's overall a very easy game but you do need to understand the core mechanics, like keeping track of your crops and not letting them wilt. Some friends of mine struggled with the fishing minigame, while I didn't have any problems at all and would even say that it's one of my favourite mini fishing games ever. It will get easier tho, when you get better equipment.
It can be hard to keep track of all the villagers and where they are at certain points in the game. Most people just look it up online, just wait until they naturally meet them or have learned over time where to look for certain NPCs.

I can see why some QoL features might be wanted for new players, that I don't necessarily need (for example a tracker on the map to see where each NPC is at the moment) but fear not. The Stardew Modding Community is big and even if you (sadly) can't just install the mods over Steam, there are a lot useful guides online on how to set things up to start your modded Stardew journey.


Have fun farming! And don't forget: we say [u] no [/u] to Joja!!!

I picked up this game after having owned it for a few years since my internet was down for a week, and my god did I get addicted to it quick. While the early game was a little slow, there was still plenty to do that didn't require energy (basically a resource meter that drains whenever you do something like swing an axe). 

The game might seem really daunting to get into, and that's a fair thing to feel, as there is an absolute mountain of content. As someone who played without any access to the wiki, let me tell you, you really don't need it to fully enjoy the game. Most things can either be figured out yourself with a bit of smart thinking and experimenting, or the answer is out there somewhere in the world, you just need to play enough to find it.

The progression in this game is really satisfying, especially with just how many ways there are to improve your farm, your efficiency, or your character's strength. For example, you start off having to manually water your crops, until you unlock sprinklers, which then opens up a ton of time and energy to be spent on other activities. Then you unlock the greenhouse, which lets you farm whatever you want regardless of the season, meaning you can throw a multi-harvest crop in there and never have to worry about money again.

The art and music of this game is gorgeous; the pixel art is really well done and pleasing to look at, and the music is an absolute treat on the ears, I personally really like the fall theme "Raven's Descent" for the flute.

The characters present all have their own unique events which can be viewed by visiting a given location under the right circumstances, such as raining at night. You can view more of these by increasing your friendship with the villagers, and it helps a lot with making them feel like real people. That being said, that does lead into my biggest complaint about the game, that being the somewhat lacking generic dialogue options.

A lot of generic actions like gifting or casually talking to villagers will lead to the same few dialogues, with some variance depending on how close you are to said villager. This did kind of hurt my immersion, as hearing someone say the exact same thing every time I gift them makes it feel more game-y. For a game that seems to put a lot of emphasis on interacting and forming bonds with the people you meet, I didn't feel super incentivized to talk with most villagers outside of getting friendship points. It's a bit of a shame, as I feel like if everyone had more dialogue it'd really help flesh out the world even more.

A smaller issue I have is that the combat isn't very good, it's pretty much entirely spamming left click. Swapping items can feel kind of clunky at times, since it's pretty easy to accidentally lock yourself into swinging your pick when you meant to swap to your sword and quickly attack, and aiming your attack is a bit of a pain since you need to make your character face the direction you want to swing, but by doing that you move yourself towards the enemy. There is mouse aiming, but you need to have your mouse basically be on top of your character for it to do anything. I understand that it's not meant to be a super combat heavy game, but that doesn't mean that the combat can't be good.

It might seem like most of this review is me talking about negatives, but that's because I'd just be repeating myself saying "the game is really good". I'm also trying to keep things vague as to avoid spoiling anything. Basically, if you want a chill game to relax with that also has a really good sense of progression, consider giving Stardew Valley a try.

Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that just stays with you. I went all the way and 100%’d it, and for some reason I still open it from time to time — sometimes just to walk around and listen to the rain, sometimes to go fight slimes in the mines like it’s a life-or-death mission. There’s something therapeutic about almost dying to a dust spirit at 2 AM.

But what really sets the game apart is the people. The characters feel like they’ve got actual lives and issues. Abigail? Eats rocks and somehow makes it cool. Haley starts off like she runs a high school mean girl cult, but ends up surprisingly decent. Shane has the emotional range of an actual human being who's seen some stuff. They’re flawed in ways that make sense, and that makes Pelican Town feel incredibly real.

And then there’s ConcernedApe! one person making an entire game of this scale and heart? No cut corners, no cash grabs, no “season pass.” Just layered design, care for the craft, and free updates even years later. The guy’s a workhorse.

Oh, and one personal tip: Don't play it with your spouse. Stardew has a weird power. One minute you're just choosing which crops to plant, next minute you're low-key angry at your partner for messing up the chests. I almost got divorced over a virtual chicken coop. Not kidding.

All in all, it's calm, deep, and has more soul than most games released today. Easily one of the best experiences I’ve ever had in gaming.

Stardew Valley is a masterpiece of the farming simulation genre. What starts as a simple farming game quickly expands into a rich experience filled with exploration, mining, fishing, crafting, cooking, animal care, festivals, and meaningful relationships with the villagers. Every season introduces new crops, events, and opportunities, making each year feel fresh.

The charming pixel art, relaxing soundtrack, and rewarding progression create a peaceful atmosphere that makes it easy to spend hours playing without noticing the time. Whether you're optimizing your farm, completing the Community Center, exploring the mines, or simply enjoying daily life in Pelican Town, there's always something meaningful to do.

Pros: Huge amount of content, relaxing gameplay, memorable characters, excellent progression, incredible replayability.

Cons: Slow beginning, some late-game grinding, limited combat depth.

When the fatigue of concrete jungles seeps into your bones, a call emerges from between the pixels—not an escape, but a return.

Stardew Valley is a love letter to the earth. It lets you touch not just soil, but the very texture of time itself. You lift your hoe at dawn, when the dew still clings to the grass, and return under a moon-washed sky as twilight bleeds into night. The seasons turn in gentle 16-bit hues: spring with its drifting cherry blossoms, summer alive with fireflies, autumn thick as maple syrup, and winter warmed by the crackle of a hearth. Here, time is not a whip at your back but a stream you can sip slowly.

Yet beneath this land runs a vein more precious than any harvest—the people, each carrying their own scars and stories. The veteran drinking alone in the bar corner, the old curator mending fragments of memory, the one-eyed boy staring at the sea from the pier… Every conversation quietly knits back the frayed threads of the community. Until one festival evening, you find yourself laughing by the bonfire, truly home.

The game’s deepest magic lies in turning labor into poetic meditation. You plant not just seeds, but days of anticipation; you catch not just fish, but the breath of an entire world beneath the waves; in the mines, each swing of the pickaxe echoes against the hidden chambers of your own heart. When your first jar of pickles matures, when a chick pecks free from its shell, a primal satisfaction stirs within—an ancient covenant between humanity and the land, diluted by modern life but never forgotten.

More astonishing is how this seemingly simple pixelated world holds quiet depths. The abandoned Community Center’s silent plea, the blue shadow of Joja Corporation, the dreams within the Wizard’s Tower… the game gently asks: as traditions fade and connections thin, how do we rebuild a sense of place? Every choice you make becomes part of the answer.

Here, success is not measured in gold, but in the laughter that returns to Pelican Town because of you—in the vintage aging in your cellar, in the coat your partner drapes over your shoulders on a rainy night. It heals not by offering an illusion, but by reminding you how to sink roots into the earth, and how to turn passing days into a life worth savoring.

So if you ever hear the rain tapping on leaves outside your window, if you still remember the scent of wet soil—then the train to Stardew Valley is arriving. Bring the parts of you that still yearn for something real, and claim your rusty hoe. A life meant to be lived slowly awaits.

Stardew Valley changed my life in ways I honestly never expected.

I am a 38 year old divorced woman with 2 kids. My life wasn’t crashing all at once—it was decaying slowly. My husband and I didn’t have explosive fights. It was worse than that. We argued about nothing. Dishes left out. Money. That awful silence at dinner where no one wants to be the first to speak. They say communication is key but we had none of that.

One night, after another pointless argument about groceries, he went to sleep on the couch. I stayed up, scrolling. That’s when I saw it.
Saw her.
Haley.
She looked so pretty. So feminine. So rude. I thought, Sure. Why not.

I named my farm after my biggest goal of the game; Haley

That’s where it all went wrong.

I started waking up early—not for work, not for my kids—but to water parsnips. I knew the villagers’ schedules better than my own family’s. I remembered birthdays. I listened. I helped. I mattered. I. MATTERED.

No one yelled at me in Pelican Town. No one judged the way I used to water my seeds everyday before I knew sprinklers even existed.

My husband asked why I was smiling at my screen at two in the morning. I didn’t answer. He wouldn't understand anyway. I was fishing. Willy needed me. My crops needed me. The community center needed me. Haley needed me.

Weeks went by.

My marriage didn’t survive the winter, but my farm did. Even though I didn't have a greenhouse, I used that as a chance to get to know the game more. A break from farming, but more foraging, mining and fishing.

When the divorce papers arrived, I felt strangely empty. I had just unlocked the greenhouse. My kids asked why I seemed distant. I told them I was “working on myself.” That wasn’t a lie. I had hit level 10 farming.

Now I live alone. My house is quiet, but my barn is full. I have truffle oil money. I have a wife who lives in my computer and loves me no matter what. I have a cat and a dog that never judges me.

Do I miss my old life? Sometimes.
Do I regret it? No.

Because when I lie in bed at night, listening to the soft Stardew Valley music, I know one thing for sure:

Haley would never treat me like that.

Stardew Valley is a game I never thought I’d enjoy, but about 150 hours later I’d say it’s one of my favorites. Despite this I never felt the urge to come back to the game, as the earlygame is a real slog until you get yourself situated with some animals, crops and sprinklers. Most of my newer save files, singleplayer or multiplayer, haven’t made it past the first two in-game weeks.

If you do decide to do what I did and replay the game, genuinely consider trying out modding. Stardew has a very active mod scene that develops everything from quality of life changes to story expansions for existing characters, from utter memes to expansive large scale mods that might was well be paid dlc. Modding reinvigorated my interest in the game, even if I’m still doing the same earlygame routine I know that there’s more content ahead. With the amount of mods the game has and continues to get, you’re bound to find something up your alley.

Amazing game on its own, definitely give it a chance even if you aren’t a fan of the genre. If you’re like me and want something fresh after enough time spent on your main save, modding is an excellent way to squeeze more hours out of this very worthwhile purchase.
